guideSummary.surfnerd: Malibu is a right-hand reefbreak tucked into a south-facing bay in Chiba, sharing its name with the Californian original but earning its own reputation as a typhoon classic. If the main peak is not cooperating, there are a few other options within the confines of the bay.

Over the southern breakwall sits a separate break called Seagull Mai, where constantly dumped old fishing nets help build up the sandbars.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Uchizuma is a small beach break that peels over sand and offers some shelter from north winds. It closes out once the surf pushes past head high, so it is one to save for the smaller days. It also works as a handy indicator for what might be firing on the nearby islands off Mugi; getting out there means renting a boat, but it can be worth the effort, since Teba is rumoured to hold a long right.

Waves more likely to be from local windswells than distant groundswells and the ideal wave angle is from the southeast. The beach break offers both left and right hand waves. It's sometimes crowded here. Dangerous rips are a hazard of surfing here.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Nii-jima's Habushiura is a consistent beachbreak that once hosted a WCT contest, and on its day it lines up and peels for long, hollow rides over sand. Both lefts and rights come through. The island has at least nine other named breaks tucked below the koga volcanic cliffs on either side, and Secrets, on the southeast corner, ranks among Japan's best waves.

Good surf at all stages of the tide. Unlikely to be too crowded, even when the surf is up.
